props.title: Jesus' Son
props.initialSlug: A junkie's surreal journey toward redemption

sections.content: Jesus' Son brilliantly captures Denis Johnson's fragmentary novel about a drug-addled drifter in 1970s America. Director Alison Maclean transforms challenging source material into a darkly comic road movie that feels like Drugstore Cowboy (1989) crossed with The Last Detail (1973). Billy Crudup delivers a career-defining performance as FH ("Fuckhead"), wandering through a haze of heroin and mystical encounters. The film's non-linear structure mirrors its protagonist's fractured consciousness, while maintaining a surprising warmth and humanity.

sections.content: What sets Jesus' Son apart from other addiction narratives is its peculiar blend of tragedy and grace. Unlike the punishing darkness of Requiem for a Dream (2000) or the clinical detachment of Clean and Sober (1988), Maclean finds moments of transcendent beauty in FH's stumbling journey toward redemption. The episodic structure allows for stunning standalone sequences - particularly the emergency room scene with Denis Leary and the surreal drive with Jack Black's pill-popping orderly.

The film shares DNA with other adaptations of Beat-adjacent literature like On the Road (2012) and Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998), but maintains a distinctly Midwestern sensibility. Its portrait of small-town desperation and occasional magic recalls Affliction (1997) and Buffalo '66 (1998), while the spiritual undertones suggest Breaking the Waves (1996). movies.title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
movies.slug: Terry Gilliam's lysergic adaptation of Hunter S. Thompson's savage journey to the heart of the American dream

sections.content: The film's second half marks a subtle shift from chaos to potential salvation, though never in expected ways. Like Clean and Sober (1988) and 28 Days (2000), it explores recovery, but through a lens of magical realism rather than twelve-step literalism. FH's work at a hospital and eventual move toward sobriety feels earned precisely because it's messy and non-linear, punctuated by setbacks and supernatural glimpses.
